{{short description|Links the homology groups of a product space with those of the individual spaces}}
In [[mathematics]], specifically in [[algebraic topology]], the '''Eilenberg–Zilber theorem''' is an important result in establishing the link between the [[homology group]]s of a [[Product topology|product space]] <math>X \times Y</math> and those of the spaces <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math>. The theorem first appeared in a 1953 paper in the [[American Journal of Mathematics]] by [[Samuel Eilenberg]] and Joseph A. Zilber.  One possible route to a proof is the [[acyclic model]] theorem.

==Statement of the theorem==
The theorem can be formulated as follows. Suppose <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> are [[topological space]]s. Then we have the three [[chain complex]]es <math>C_*(X)</math>, <math>C_*(Y)</math>, and <math>C_*(X \times Y) </math>. (The argument applies equally to the [[Simplex|simplicial]] or singular chain complexes.) We also have the ''[[tensor product]] complex'' <math>C_*(X) \otimes C_*(Y)</math>, whose differential is, by definition, 
:<math>\partial_{C_*(X) \otimes C_*(Y)}( \sigma \otimes \tau) = \partial_X \sigma \otimes \tau + (-1)^p \sigma \otimes \partial_Y\tau</math>

for <math>\sigma \in C_p(X)</math> and <math>\partial_X</math>, <math>\partial_Y</math> the differentials on <math>C_*(X)</math>,<math>C_*(Y)</math>.

Then the theorem says that we have [[chain complex#Chain maps|chain maps]]

:<math>F\colon C_*(X \times Y) \rightarrow C_*(X) \otimes C_*(Y), \quad G\colon C_*(X) \otimes C_*(Y) \rightarrow C_*(X \times Y)</math>

such that <math>FG</math> is the identity and <math>GF</math> is [[Homotopy category of chain complexes|chain-homotopic]] to the identity. Moreover, the maps are [[natural transformation|natural]] in <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math>. Consequently the two complexes must have the same [[Homology (mathematics)|homology]]:

:<math>H_*(C_*(X \times Y)) \cong H_*(C_*(X) \otimes C_*(Y)).</math>

==Statement in terms of composite maps==

The original theorem was proven in terms of acyclic models but explicit formulas for the map <math>G</math> and the homotopy <math>H</math> were later found by Eilenberg and Mac Lane. The standard map <math>F</math> they produce is traditionally referred to as the '''Alexander&ndash;Whitney map''' and <math>G</math> the '''Eilenberg&ndash;Zilber map'''. The maps are natural in both <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> and inverse up to homotopy: one has

:<math>FG = \mathrm{id}_{C_*(X) \otimes C_*(Y)}, \qquad GF - \mathrm{id}_{C_*(X \times Y)} = \partial_{C_*(X) \otimes C_*(Y)}H+H\partial_{C_*(X) \otimes C_*(Y)}</math>

for a homotopy <math>H</math> natural in both <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> such that further, each of <math>HH</math>, <math>FH</math>, and <math>HG</math> is zero. This is what would come to be known as a ''contraction'' or a ''homotopy retract datum''.

==The coproduct==

The diagonal map <math>\Delta\colon X \to X \times X</math> induces a map of cochain complexes <math>C_*(X) \to C_*(X \times X)</math> which, followed by the Alexander&ndash;Whitney <math>F</math> yields a coproduct <math>C_*(X) \to C_*(X) \otimes C_*(X)</math> inducing the standard coproduct on <math>H_*(X)</math>. With respect to these coproducts on 
<math>X</math> and <math>Y</math>, the map 

:<math>H_*(X) \otimes H_*(Y) \to H_*\big(C_*(X) \otimes C_*(Y)\big)\ \overset\sim\to\ H_*(X \times Y)</math>,

also called the Eilenberg&ndash;Zilber map, becomes a map of [[differential graded coalgebra]]s. The composite <math>C_*(X) \to C_*(X) \otimes C_*(X)</math> itself is not a map of coalgebras.

==Statement in cohomology==

The Alexander&ndash;Whitney and Eilenberg&ndash;Zilber maps dualize (over any choice of commutative coefficient ring <math>k</math> with unity) to a pair of maps

:<math>G^*\colon C^*(X \times Y) \rightarrow \big(C_*(X) \otimes C_*(Y)\big)^*, \quad F^*\colon \big(C_*(X) \otimes C_*(Y)\big)^*\rightarrow C^*(X \times Y)</math>

which are also homotopy equivalences, as witnessed by the duals of the preceding equations, using the dual homotopy <math>H^*</math>. The coproduct does not dualize straightforwardly, because dualization does not distribute over tensor products of infinitely-generated modules, but there is a natural injection of [[differential graded algebra]]s <math>i\colon C^*(X) \otimes C^*(Y) \to \big(C_*(X) \otimes C_*(Y)\big)^*</math> given by <math>\alpha \otimes \beta \mapsto (\sigma \otimes \tau \mapsto \alpha(\sigma)\beta(\tau))</math>, the product being taken in the coefficient ring <math>k</math>. This <math>i</math> induces an isomorphism in cohomology, so one does have the zig-zag of differential graded algebra maps 

:<math> C^*(X) \otimes C^*(X)\ \overset{i}{\to}\ \big(C_*(X) \otimes C_*(X)\big)^*\ \overset{G^*}{\leftarrow}\ C^*(X \times X) \overset{C^*(\Delta)}{\to} C^*(X)</math>

inducing a product <math>\smile\colon H^*(X) \otimes H^*(X) \to H^*(X)</math> in cohomology, known as the [[cup product]], because <math>H^*(i)</math> and <math>H^*(G)</math> are isomorphisms. Replacing <math>G^*</math> with <math>F^*</math> so the maps all go the same way, one gets the standard cup product on cochains, given explicitly by 

:<math>\alpha \otimes \beta \mapsto \Big(\sigma \mapsto (\alpha \otimes \beta)(F^*\Delta^*\sigma) =
\sum_{p=0}^{\dim \sigma} \alpha(\sigma|_{\Delta^{[0,p]}}) \cdot \beta(\sigma|_{\Delta^{[p,\dim \sigma]}})\Big)</math>,

which, since cochain evaluation <math>C^p(X) \otimes C_q(X) \to k</math> vanishes unless <math>p=q</math>, reduces to the more familiar expression.

Note that if this direct map <math>C^*(X) \otimes C^*(X) \to C^*(X)</math> of cochain complexes were in fact a map of differential graded algebras, then the cup product would make <math>C^*(X)</math> a [[Graded-commutative_ring|commutative graded algebra]], which it is not. This failure of the Alexander&ndash;Whitney map to be a [[coalgebra]] map is an example the unavailability of commutative cochain-level models for cohomology over fields of nonzero characteristic, and thus is in a way responsible for much of the subtlety and complication in [[stable homotopy theory]].

==Generalizations==

An important generalisation to the [[non-abelian group|non-abelian]] case using crossed complexes is given in the paper by Andrew Tonks below. This give full details of a result on the (simplicial) [[classifying space]] of a crossed complex stated but not proved in the paper by [[Ronald Brown (mathematician)|Ronald Brown]] and Philip J. Higgins on classifying spaces.

==Consequences==
The Eilenberg–Zilber theorem is a key ingredient in establishing the [[Künneth theorem]], which expresses the homology groups <math>H_*(X \times Y)</math> in terms of <math>H_*(X)</math> and <math>H_*(Y)</math>. In light of the Eilenberg–Zilber theorem, the content of the Künneth theorem consists in analysing how the homology of the tensor product complex relates to the homologies of the factors.
